headline: Two Dan Sullivans on Alaska's ballot. The FBI is asking.
summary: Alaska votes Tuesday with two Dan Sullivans on its Senate ballot: the Republican senator and a retired teacher. The FBI is visiting the teacher's donors to ask whether they were misled. Two who were asked said they knew who they gave to. Prosecutors cite a report that Mary Peltola's campaign recruited him. She calls it garbage.

cover_question.q: Is it a crime to share a name?

cover_answer: No. The question is whether anyone meant to fool voters.
table_question: Two kids, one name. Who has to go by their middle name?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: In Alaska, two men named Dan Sullivan want the same job, like two kids in one class with the same name. The FBI is asking people who gave money to one of them if they got mixed up. One man said no, he knew just who he picked. The grown-ups are sorting it out.
5-7.why: Two kids with one name is a problem they have met. Who's investigating whom can wait; a six-year-old follows one mix-up at a time, so the script gives them one.
5-7.why_long: A child this age reasons from what is in front of them, and two kids in one class with the same name is in front of them most days. The script hands them that and nothing else: no election, no FBI beyond people asking a question. Expect "which one is the real Dan?" Say both are, and that is the whole problem.

8-12.script: Alaska votes Tuesday. Sen. Dan Sullivan is running, and so is Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher. After a report that his rival's campaign recruited him, the FBI is asking his donors if they meant to back him, like a referee checking a team sheet. Two said yes.
8-12.why: Same name, possible mix-up, somebody checks. That is a rules question, and this age wants to know who checks and whether the check is fair.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out rules and whether adults apply them evenly, so the script runs the chain: same name, a report of a plan, a check on the donors. The referee is the checker they know. Expect "so was it a trick?" Say nobody knows yet, two donors said they weren't tricked, and the FBI has charged no one.

13-17.script: Is it a crime to share a name with the senator? Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher, is on Alaska's ballot beside Sen. Dan Sullivan, and the FBI is asking his donors if they were fooled. Second: agents at your door days before a vote. Fair check, or a thumb on the scale?
13-17.why: A fair probe and a badly timed one can be the same probe. They can hold both now. Let them say which weighs more before you do.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: a candidate planted to confuse voters would be a real fraud, and FBI agents at donors' doors days before a vote is real pressure on it. The script asks them to weigh the two, which is the argument the adults are having. Expect "which side are you on?" Say what you think, and why.

5-7.q: Why did the FBI go to a boat shop?
5-7.a: To find a man who gave money to the teacher and ask if he mixed up the two Dans. He said he didn't.

8-12.q: Can two people have the same name?
8-12.a: Anyone who qualifies can run. The teacher uses his middle initial.

8-12.q: Did donors give to the wrong Dan?
8-12.a: The FBI is asking. One man who gave $500 said he knew who he backed.

13-17.q: Is it a crime to share a name?
13-17.a: No. The question is whether anyone meant to fool voters.

13-17.q: Isn't this intimidating, right before an election?
13-17.a: Peltola calls it a smear. Prosecutors say the probe began months ago.
